title: The Art of Value Investing | John Heins & Whitney Tilson | Talks at Google
description:
“John Heins and Whitney Tilson, co-founders of the Value Investor Insight newsletter, have done a thorough job of explaining how to look for stocks that are trading at significant discounts to what they are worth — the concept known as the value style of investing.…the authors present a clear framework for ferreting out undervalued companies.”
—The New York Times

About the book:
In The Art of Value Investing, John Heins and Whitney Tilson offer a comprehensive set of answers to the questions that everyone investing seriously in the stock market should have thought through clearly before committing his or her hard-earned capital to the endeavor. What market efficiencies will I try to exploit? What analytical edge can I hope to have? How specifically will I decide to buy or sell? For answers, they call on market-beating money managers – including such investing luminaries as Seth Klarman, David Einhorn, Bill Ackman, Howard Marks, Mason Hawkins and Julian Robertson – who have graced the pages over the past ten years of their highly regarded newsletter, Value Investor Insight. To illustrate one of the equity investor’s most important tasks – how to value a company – they will present a particularly relevant current case study … on Google.
 
About the authors:
John Heins is the co-founder and President of Value Investor Media, Inc. and Editor-in-Chief of Value Investor Insight and SuperInvestor Insight. Previously, he served as CEO of Bertelsmann AG’s U.S. magazine subsidiary, ran AOL’s Personal Finance business and was a reporter and staff writer for Forbes magazine. He holds a bachelor’s degree in Economics from the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School and earned an M.B.A. from Stanford University.

summary: The speakers argue that Google's core business is exceptionally high-quality and profitable, noting that its stock appears undervalued because significant investments in new ventures are expensed rather than capitalized. They believe the company possesses a strong moat and a virtuous cycle, with potential for significant growth driven by both core revenue expansion and future innovations like self-driving cars. While acknowledging past mistakes in shorting the company, the speakers maintain a bullish stance on its long-term trajectory and global game-changing potential.

claims.claim: The speaker believes Google's core business is highly profitable and that the stock is not as expensive as it appears due to expensed investments in new ventures.
claims.quote: And then they're investing in a lot of new stuff where there's likelihood to pay off. So this gives you a sense-- by the way, again, what I sort of missed is is companies that have a lot of optionality to get into new businesses, make acquisitions, et cetera.
claims.speaker: John Heins

claims.claim: The speaker argues that Google's core business is actually much more profitable than it appears because they expense a lot of their investments in new ventures.
claims.quote: So what is it saying is we're in the market probably 16 times earnings for the S&P 500. So any way you could it you guys are at some premium to that, but not a crazy premium.
claims.speaker: John Heins

claims.claim: The speaker thinks Google is a high-quality company where he would be willing to double his money in four years with low risk of downside.
claims.quote: If I thought this stock was very likely, with low risk of downside, very likely to be a double in four years, I don't know all day, on a real high quality company where I think I can double my money in for years.
claims.speaker: John Heins

claims.claim: The speaker states that he certainly would not bet against Google stock given its growth trajectory and quality.
claims.quote: That's pretty rare, but you guys have been doing it. So I certainly wouldn't bet against it.
claims.speaker: John Heins

claims.claim: The speaker notes that Google has a worldwide game changer potential with self-driving cars which could change the world.
claims.quote: If you guys nail that, that could change the world. That's a worldwide game changer, and you guys will own it.
claims.speaker: John Heins

claims.claim: The speaker suggests that Google's core business is trading at a reasonable multiple of 15 times earnings if you exclude expenses from non-revenue generating ventures.
claims.quote: And you might actually say Google's core business trading for 15 times earnings or something like a market multiple, and then you're getting a free call option on stuff that-- self-driving cars.
claims.speaker: John Heins

claims.claim: The speaker believes that if Google continues to grow revenues at 20% for the next four years with flat margins, the stock could double in four years.
claims.quote: You continue to grow your revenues 20% for the next four years, if your margins just stay flat, that means the earnings go up 20% a year. That's a double in four years.
claims.speaker: John Heins

claims.claim: The speaker is intrigued by Google and plans to do more work on it despite its large market cap.
claims.quote: I'm actually sort of intrigued with Google. The other thing, by the way, is it's such a big company with such a large market cap it's hard to make a lot of money buying things with multi-hundred billion market caps.
claims.speaker: John Heins

claims.claim: The speaker admits that he was initially wrong about Google's growth but now appreciates its virtuous cycle and moat.
claims.quote: And I missed the very powerful virtuous cycle at work with Google. A large user base translates into large advertiser base, better monetization, more R&D dollars, yielding a better product, which a better product is a high barrier to entry, which then attracts more of a user base, et cetera.
claims.speaker: John Heins

claims.claim: The speaker states that he never lost any money on Google stock, although he did not make any money on it either.
claims.quote: OK, so I've never lost any money on Google. I just haven't made any money on it.
claims.speaker: John Heins

claims.claim: The speaker believes that Google's core business is one of the world's greatest businesses.
claims.quote: One of the world's greatest businesses. And then they're investing in a lot of new stuff where there's likelihood to pay off.
claims.speaker: John Heins

claims.claim: The speaker believes that Google's core business is actually even much more profitable than it appears because they expense a lot of their investments in new ventures.
claims.quote: So what is it saying is we're in the market probably 16 times earnings for the S&P 500. So any way you could it you guys are at some premium to that, but not a crazy premium.
claims.speaker: John Heins

claims.claim: The speaker admits to making a mistake by holding Google stock for years while reading negative news, eventually selling after a small gain.
claims.quote: I'll admit, when he's talking about his stupid mistake with Google, I had Apple stock. And my son, who is now 22 years old, when he was born. I put it in his college savings fund. And I had Apple stock that did nothing for years.
claims.speaker: JOHN HEINS

claims.claim: The speaker admits to shorting Tesla but later gained appreciation for it and thinks it is an incredible company.
claims.quote: Well, compare that to a Tesla, which is I was stupid enough to short, and then gained appreciation for it and think it's an incredible company. But you see, they actually have to make stuff, and then they have to ship it, and they have inventory, et cetera, et cetera.
claims.speaker: WHITNEY TILSON

claims.claim: The speaker believes Facebook has the greatest business model in the world, being a winner-take-all business with zero incremental cost to add members.
claims.quote: I actually think Facebook may well have the greatest business model in the world. It's a winner-take-all business. It's one out of every six people on the planet is now a member. And it costs them nothing to add new members. There's zero incremental cost, so they just grow globally at no incremental cost, and it's just pure profit.
claims.speaker: WHITNEY TILSON

claims.claim: The speaker mentions Amazon in the context of a question about supercomputers interfering in the market, but does not express a specific investment view on the company.
claims.quote: And maybe supercomputers, the way they interfere in the market now, may be amplifying this by reacting to momentum, et cetera. So with the value of a company being so skewed sometimes over a very long time, is value investing harder or less effective these days?
claims.speaker: AUDIENCE

claims.claim: The speaker notes that the crowd was right on Google and that the stock was an 11-bagger, implying it was undervalued.
claims.quote: The crowd was right on Google. If anything, the crowd didn't appreciate Google enough. We now know, stock was an 11-bagger.
claims.speaker: Whitney Tilson

claims.claim: The speaker admits Netflix was a massively better company than he thought and that his short thesis pillars were wrong.
claims.quote: Netflix was a massively better company than I thought. And the key pillars of my short thesis were there's no moat around the business, and sort of wacky management, and competitors are going to come in and eat their lunch. All of my pillars of my short thesis were wrong.
claims.speaker: Whitney Tilson

claims.claim: The speaker mentions Costco's low cost service as an example of a competitive moat he was trained to think about.
claims.quote: And I was trained to think about the competitive moats of companies-- Coke's brand or Costco's low cost service or whatever.
claims.speaker: Whitney Tilson

claims.claim: The speaker mentions Meta as an example of a tech stock he was trained not to look at.
claims.quote: You don't look at tech stocks, et cetera, et cetera.
claims.speaker: Whitney Tilson

claims.claim: The speaker views Netflix as a potential world-beater that made a bold bet to invest in streaming content despite short-term profitability losses.
claims.quote: Netflix, they were selling an earnings growth story, and then they decided the hell with earnings growth, hell with earnings at all. We're just going to invest in the future. We're become like Amazon. And all the investors that were in there for the earnings interest story sold the stock. But I was like, you know what, I think this company could be a world beater someday.
claims.speaker: WHITNEY TILSON

claims.claim: The speaker notes that Amazon has never made a profit because of its policy of plowing every penny of profit back into future growth.
claims.quote: Amazon's been doing that for 20 years. They've never made a profit because they have a policy of taking every single penny of profit and plowing it back in to future growth. And you know what, the market hasn't destroyed Amazon stock.
claims.speaker: WHITNEY TILSON
